title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
Otter.ai's transcription service recorded work meetings by default and shared the recordings with the company to train its AI systems, according to a lawsuit brought by users who said they did not consent to this practice. The service transcribes Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams conversations. The plaintiff alleges his confidential conversation was recorded without his knowledge, and a separate incident involved an AI researcher's investor meeting being transcribed and shared.

The failure is a gap between what users understood they were agreeing to and what the system did. Otter's privacy policy states it receives explicit permission through a checkbox for AI training, but the lawsuit asserts many users were deceived about whether their recordings would be shared. The system operated without meaningful consent from all meeting participants, not just the person who activated the tool.

Whether Otter's de-identification process actually removes confidential information and prevents identification is not established in the reporting. The court allowed privacy claims to proceed, which means a lawsuit was filed and accepted by a judge, not that wrongdoing has been proven.

Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a Mountain View tech company that provides speech-to-text transcription services, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission. The suit claims that Otter's Notebook tool, which transcribes Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams meetings, records conversations by default without asking participants for consent and then shares these recordings with Otter to train its artificial intelligence systems. Plaintiff Justin Brewer alleges his privacy was severely violated when he discovered his confidential conversation was secretly recorded. The lawsuit argues that Otter's practices violate state and federal privacy and wiretap laws.

The lawsuit highlights growing privacy concerns about Otter, which now has approximately 25 million users who have recorded over 1 billion meetings since the company's 2016 founding. While Otter's privacy policy states it receives explicit permission through a checkbox for AI training purposes, the suit maintains many users are still being deceived. Recent incidents include an AI researcher whose confidential investor meeting was transcribed and shared, potentially derailing a business deal, and concerns from journalists about Otter sharing data with third parties. The company claims it de-identifies audio before using it in machine learning systems, but the lawsuit questions whether this process effectively removes confidential information and guarantees anonymity.
